lessons.title: When someone can bind you without asking
lessons.summary: An agent acts for a principal and can make contracts that bind them. The dangerous part is that authority can look real to an outsider even when it was never given.

sections.keypoint: A contract can be made for you by someone else, and it binds you as if you signed.
sections.h: A shop manager orders forty crates

body.text: Encik Zainal owns a hardware shop in Seremban. He employs a manager, Lim, to run it while he is away.
Lim orders forty crates of tile adhesive from a supplier. He signs nothing in his own name. The invoice comes to Zainal.
Zainal never saw the order. He is still bound by it. That is agency.
The law lets one person make contracts for another. The person acting is the agent. The person bound is the principal.

sections.keypoint: Authority can be given in words, implied from a role, or created by appearances.
sections.h: Three ways authority arises

body.text: The question in almost every agency dispute is whether the agent had authority. There is more than one way to have it.

body.caption: How an agent comes to have authority
rows: Express
Said or written by the principal
"Order the adhesive."
Implied
Comes with the job the agent was given
A shop manager may order ordinary stock.
Apparent
Created by how the principal made things look
The principal let Lim order for a year and never objected.
body.alt: Three kinds of authority. Express authority comes from what the principal said or wrote, such as an instruction to order the adhesive. Implied authority comes with the job given, so a shop manager may order ordinary stock. Apparent authority is created by how the principal made things look to outsiders, such as allowing an agent to order for a year without objecting.

body.text: The third one causes the trouble. It can exist when the principal never agreed to anything.

sections.keypoint: A private instruction the supplier never saw does not shrink what the supplier may rely on.
sections.h: The secret limit that does not work

body.text: Suppose Zainal told Lim privately never to order more than ten crates.
The supplier does not know that. It has dealt with Lim for a year. From outside, Lim looks like a manager who may order stock.

Where a principal holds a person out as having authority, a third party who deals with them in good faith may rely on that appearance. A private limit the third party did not know about does not bind them.
body.source: Doctrine of apparent authority; the general law of agency in Malaysia is in the Contracts Act 1950.

body.text: So Zainal is bound to the supplier. His remedy is against Lim, for exceeding what he was told.
Notice the two relationships. The principal and agent have one contract. The principal and third party have another. Breaking the first does not undo the second.

sections.keypoint: An agent owes loyalty, not just competence, and may not profit secretly.
sections.h: What the agent owes back

body.text: Authority runs one way. Duty runs the other.

items: **Obey instructions.** Act within what was actually authorised.
**Act with care.** Use the skill the role calls for.
**No secret profit.** An agent who takes a commission from the supplier without telling the principal must account for it.
**No conflict.** Do not act for both sides without disclosure and consent.

body.text: The last two are the ones examiners test. They are duties of loyalty, and they are strict.

body.prompt: Lim takes RM500 from the supplier for choosing them. The price to Zainal was still fair. Has Lim breached anything?
body.reveal: Yes. The duty is not to avoid loss but to avoid undisclosed profit. That the price was fair is an answer to a claim for damages, not to the claim for the RM500.

quiz.q: A shop manager orders ordinary stock without being told to. What kind of authority is that?
options: Express authority
Implied authority, because it comes with the job
No authority at all
Authority only if the principal later agrees
quiz.why: Implied authority is what comes with the role. A manager engaged to run a shop may do the ordinary things running a shop requires.

quiz.q: A principal privately caps an agent at ten crates. The agent orders forty from a supplier who does not know of the cap. Who is bound?
options: Nobody, because the agent exceeded authority
The agent personally, and not the principal
The principal, because the supplier could rely on the appearance of authority
The supplier, who should have checked
quiz.why: A private limit the third party never knew about does not shrink what they may rely on. The principal's remedy is against the agent.

quiz.q: An agent takes an undisclosed commission but gets the principal a fair price. What follows?
options: The agent must account for the commission, because the duty is against undisclosed profit
Nothing, because the principal suffered no loss
The contract with the third party is automatically void
The principal must first prove bad faith
quiz.why: Loyalty duties are strict. Absence of loss answers a damages claim; it does not answer the claim to the secret profit itself.

lessons.source: The general law of agency in Malaysia is contained in the Contracts Act 1950. The categories of authority and the agent's duties as described here are standard agency doctrine.
lessons.verify: This lesson deliberately gives no section numbers. Read the agency provisions of the Contracts Act 1950 directly and check each proposition against the section text before relying on it.

reading.where: the agency provisions — read them beside the lesson's categories of authority, and notice that the Act, not the case law, is the starting point
the agency chapters — the Act states the rule, the text shows how the courts have read it

lessons.title: Being sacked, and what the law does about it
lessons.summary: Malaysian employment law runs on two tracks: a statute setting minimum terms for certain employees, and a separate system for challenging a dismissal without just cause.

sections.keypoint: Losing a job raises two different questions, answered by two different systems.
sections.h: Two questions, not one

body.text: Puan Faridah has worked at a factory in Klang for six years. On Monday she is told not to come back.
She has two separate questions, and people mix them up constantly.

items: **Was I paid what I was owed?** Notice, overtime, leave, termination benefits.
**Should I have been dismissed at all?** Whether there was a good reason, and whether it was done fairly.

body.text: The first is about minimum terms. The second is about the dismissal itself. Different law, different forum.

sections.keypoint: The Employment Act sets a floor, and who stands on that floor is defined.
sections.h: The statutory floor

body.text: The first question is answered mostly by statute.

The Employment Act 1955 sets minimum terms of employment — matters such as hours, rest days, leave and notice. Its protections apply to employees who fall within its scope, which the Act itself defines.
Two things matter here. A contract cannot give less than the statutory minimum. And who is covered is a question you must actually check.
Do not assume everyone in Malaysia is covered by every provision. Scope has changed over time, and Sabah and Sarawak have had their own ordinances.

sections.keypoint: Unfair dismissal runs through the industrial relations system, not the ordinary courts.
sections.h: The second track

body.text: The second question does not go to the High Court in the first instance.

The Industrial Relations Act 1967 provides a route for a workman dismissed without just cause or excuse to seek reinstatement. A representation is made, conciliation is attempted, and the matter may be referred to the Industrial Court.
The remedy the system is built around is reinstatement — getting the job back. Compensation is what is usually awarded instead.
There is a time limit for making the representation, and it is short. Missing it is the commonest way a good claim dies.

sections.keypoint: The employer must show a real reason and a fair procedure. Both, not either.
sections.h: What an employer has to show

body.text: "Just cause or excuse" has two halves, and an employer must satisfy both.

body.caption: The two halves of a lawful dismissal
rows: Substantive
Was there a real reason — misconduct, poor performance, redundancy?
Dismissal without cause.
Procedural
Was the employee told the case and given a chance to answer?
Dismissal unfair even if the reason was true.
body.alt: A lawful dismissal has two halves. The substantive half asks whether there was a real reason such as misconduct, poor performance or redundancy; failing it means dismissal without cause. The procedural half asks whether the employee was told the case against them and given a chance to answer. Failing it makes the dismissal unfair even where the reason was true.

body.prompt: An employee really did steal, but was dismissed with no hearing at all. Is the dismissal safe?
body.reveal: Not automatically. A true reason does not cure an absent procedure. The theft goes to the substantive half; the missing hearing goes to the procedural one, and the employer must satisfy both.

quiz.q: Which statute sets minimum terms such as leave, rest days and notice?
options: The Industrial Relations Act 1967
The Employment Act 1955
The Contracts Act 1950
The Civil Law Act 1956
quiz.why: The Employment Act 1955 sets the statutory floor. The Industrial Relations Act 1967 deals with dismissal without just cause, which is a different question.

quiz.q: Where does a claim for dismissal without just cause or excuse begin?
options: In the High Court by writ
Through a representation under the industrial relations system
In the Sessions Court
In the Syariah court if the employee is Muslim
quiz.why: The Industrial Relations Act 1967 route starts with a representation and conciliation, and may be referred on to the Industrial Court.

quiz.q: An employer proves the misconduct but held no hearing. What is the likely position?
options: The dismissal is safe, because the reason was true
The employee must sue for breach of contract instead
The Employment Act 1955 decides it
The dismissal may still be unfair, because procedure is a separate requirement
quiz.why: Just cause has a substantive and a procedural half, and an employer must satisfy both. A true reason does not cure an absent procedure.

quiz.q: What remedy is the unfair dismissal system built around?
options: Damages for distress
Reinstatement, with compensation commonly awarded instead
A criminal penalty on the employer
An injunction against the employer
quiz.why: The statutory aim is to put the workman back in the job. In practice compensation is usually awarded in place of reinstatement.

lessons.source: Employment Act 1955 for minimum terms; Industrial Relations Act 1967 for dismissal without just cause or excuse. The substantive and procedural limbs are standard industrial relations doctrine.
lessons.verify: No section numbers or time limits are stated here on purpose. Check the current scope of the Employment Act 1955, the representation time limit under the Industrial Relations Act 1967, and the position in Sabah and Sarawak, against the statutes themselves.

lessons.title: Standard terms, and the limits of freedom of contract
lessons.summary: Commercial parties draft their own rules. The Contracts Act sets the outer boundary, and a term outside it is void however carefully it was negotiated.

sections.h: Freedom, with a boundary
sections.keypoint: Commercial parties set most of their own terms, but the statute fixes an outer limit that negotiation cannot move.

body.text: Commercial law lets parties write their own rules. That is most of its usefulness.
But not everything agreed is enforceable. The Contracts Act draws a boundary, and a term outside it fails regardless of how freely it was agreed.
So a commercial drafting question has two parts. What do we want the term to do, and is it a term the law will give effect to?

Section 10(1) sets out the conditions on which an agreement becomes a contract. The parties must consent freely, and each of them must be competent. What is given in return, and the purpose the arrangement serves, must each be lawful. And the agreement must not be one that the Act elsewhere declares void. Every condition has to hold at the same time, which is why the subsection repays being read slowly.

sections.h: Read section 10(1) as a checklist
sections.keypoint: Section 10(1) is a list of conditions, and each one is a separate place a commercial agreement can fail.

body.text: That provision is easy to read as a single sentence about validity. It is more useful read as a list.
Free consent. Competence. Lawful consideration. Lawful object. Not expressly declared void.
Each is a separate requirement and each can fail on its own. In a commercial dispute, identifying which one is in issue is most of the analysis.
The last limb is the one people forget. Some agreements are void because the Act says so elsewhere, not because anything is wrong with the consent.

body.prompt: Two sophisticated companies negotiate at length, with lawyers, and agree a term the Act expressly declares void. Is it enforceable?
options: No — an express declaration of voidness is not displaced by the quality of the negotiation
Yes — they were commercial parties with equal bargaining power and full advice
body.reveal: Bargaining equality is an argument about consent, and consent is a different limb. Where the Act declares a class of agreement void, the care taken in reaching it is beside the point.

sections.h: Unlawful object and consideration
sections.keypoint: Section 24 sets out when consideration or object is unlawful, and it reaches further than obvious illegality.

body.text: Section 24 sets out the limbs on which the consideration or object of an agreement is unlawful, and provides that every agreement whose object or consideration is unlawful is void.
The limbs are worth reading one at a time. They are not all about breaking the law.
Some reach arrangements that are lawful in themselves but defeat something the law provides for. That is where commercial agreements are most likely to be caught unexpectedly.
The consequence matters too. Void is not the same as unenforceable at the option of one party. Neither side can sue on it.
Do not paraphrase the limbs from a textbook. They are precisely worded, and an argument that quotes the wrong limb is an argument about the wrong thing.

sections.h: Where the Act declares a class void
sections.keypoint: Section 26 makes agreements without consideration void as a class, subject to stated exceptions.

body.text: Section 26 is the clearest example of the fifth limb of section 10(1) in operation.
Section 26 provides that an agreement made without consideration is void, subject to the exceptions the section sets out, and it carries illustrations.
Read the exceptions, and read the illustrations. Illustrations are part of how the section is understood, and they are more concrete than anything a summary will give you.
Commercially, this matters most in variations and in promises to accept less. Those are exactly the situations where consideration is thin.

body.q: A supplier agrees to accept less than the contract price, with nothing given in return. Which provision do you reach for first?
options: Section 10(1), because consent was free
Section 26, and then its exceptions
body.why: The question is whether an agreement without consideration is enforceable, which is what section 26 addresses directly. Section 10(1) tells you validity has conditions; section 26 is the condition in issue.

quiz.q: Why is section 10(1) better read as a checklist than as a definition?
options: Because it is shorter that way
Because definitions are not binding
Because each requirement can fail independently, and identifying which is in issue is the analysis
Because it only applies to commercial contracts
quiz.why: Free consent, competence, lawful consideration, lawful object and not being declared void are separate conditions. A dispute is almost always about one of them, and naming which one is what makes an answer specific.

quiz.q: Two commercial parties with equal bargaining power agree a term the Act expressly declares void. What follows?
options: It binds them, because both consented freely
It is void — the quality of consent does not save an agreement the Act declares void
It binds only the party who drafted it
It is enforceable if the contract says so
quiz.why: Consent and express voidness are different limbs of section 10(1). Satisfying one does not answer the other.

reading.where: section 10(1), then section 24 and section 26 with its illustrations — read the illustrations, they are part of the section
the chapters on legality and on consideration, for the Malaysian treatment rather than the English one

lessons.source: Contracts Act 1950, ss 10(1), 24 and 26 — each of which is the subject of a guided reading in this corpus. No case is cited.
lessons.verify: Read sections 10(1), 24 and 26 in the current published version and check the currency date on the reprint's front matter. The Contracts Act's official consolidation may be many years old; confirm the limbs of section 24 from the section itself.

lessons.title: What a broken commercial contract is worth
lessons.summary: Section 74 governs compensation for breach. Section 75 governs a sum the contract itself names. They are different questions, and commercial contracts usually raise the second.

sections.h: Two provisions, two questions
sections.keypoint: Compensation for loss and a sum the contract names are governed separately, and confusing them is the common error.

body.text: A commercial contract is broken. There are two quite different routes to a figure.
The first asks what loss the breach caused. The second asks what the contract itself said would be payable.
The Act deals with them in separate sections, and the answers can differ.
An answer that runs them together produces a number with no route to it. Say which section you are under before you calculate anything.

sections.h: Compensation for loss
sections.keypoint: Section 74 compensates for loss naturally arising or in the parties' contemplation, and excludes remote loss.

body.text: Section 74(1) entitles the injured party to compensation for loss or damage caused which naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach, or which the parties knew when they made the contract to be likely to result. Section 74(2) excludes compensation for remote and indirect loss.
Two limbs, and they do different work. The first is about ordinary consequences. The second is about what these parties knew.
That second limb is why commercial parties disclose unusual exposure at the time of contracting. Knowledge at formation is what brings it in.
Telling the other side afterwards does not help. The section fixes the moment.

body.prompt: A buyer has an unusually lucrative sub-sale and tells the seller about it a week after the contract is signed. The seller breaches. Is the sub-sale profit recoverable under the second limb?
options: Not under that limb — it asks what the parties knew when they made the contract
Yes — the seller knew about it before breaching
body.reveal: The limb is tied to the time of contracting, because that is when the party could have priced or refused the risk. Later knowledge may matter for other purposes, but it does not retrofit contemplation.

sections.h: When the contract names a sum
sections.keypoint: Section 75 governs a sum named in the contract, and the section sets its own test rather than importing one.

body.text: Commercial contracts routinely name a figure payable on breach. Liquidated damages clauses, service credits, deposits.
Section 75 deals with the case where a sum is named in the contract as payable on breach, or the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty.
Note what the section does not do. It does not simply enforce the named figure, and it does not simply strike it down.
Read the words carefully rather than importing a test you remember from elsewhere. This is a codified provision, and the code governs.

The relationship between the named sum and proof of actual loss under this section has been the subject of Malaysian appellate decisions and the position has developed. Do not state it from memory or from an English textbook.

sections.h: Drafting with the sections in view
sections.keypoint: A clause drafted without regard to which section governs it may produce a figure the court will not award.

body.text: This is where doctrine becomes drafting. A clause that names a sum invites section 75.
A clause that instead defines what counts as recoverable loss is operating in section 74's territory.
Neither is automatically better. But drafting one while expecting the other's treatment is how commercial clauses disappoint.

body.q: Your client wants certainty about what a breach will cost. What is the honest advice?
options: A named sum engages section 75, so the figure is not automatically the amount recoverable; certainty is limited by what the section allows
Name a large sum in the contract — certainty is achieved by drafting
body.why: Naming a figure changes which section governs, not whether the court will scrutinise it. Advice that promises certainty from drafting alone has not read the provision the drafting attracts.

quiz.q: Under the second limb of section 74(1), when must the parties have known of the likely loss?
options: At any time before the breach
When the loss was suffered
When they made the contract
When proceedings were commenced
quiz.why: The limb is fixed to the time of contracting, which is when a party could have priced or declined the risk. Knowledge acquired later does not bring the loss within it.

quiz.q: A commercial contract names a sum payable on breach. Which provision governs?
options: Section 75
Section 74
Section 10(1)
Section 26
quiz.why: Section 75 addresses a sum named in the contract as payable on breach. Section 74 governs compensation for loss caused, which is a different question and can produce a different figure.

reading.where: section 74 with its explanation, then section 75 — read them consecutively, because the difference between them is the lesson
the chapter on remedies, and specifically the treatment of section 75, where the Malaysian position differs from the English one

lessons.source: Contracts Act 1950, ss 74 and 75 — both the subject of guided readings in this corpus. No case is cited, and the development of the section 75 position is deliberately left to the reader to check.
lessons.verify: Read sections 74 and 75 in the current published version and check the reprint's currency date. The section 75 position has been developed by Malaysian appellate decisions; confirm the current authority before advising on any named sum.

lessons.title: Employee or contractor, and why the label does not decide
lessons.summary: Whether someone is an employee decides which statutes apply to them at all. The contract's own description of the relationship is evidence, not the answer.

sections.h: The question that comes first
sections.keypoint: Employment protections attach to employees, so status decides whether any of the statutory regime applies.

body.text: Every employment protection begins with a category. It protects employees.
So before any question about dismissal, terms or remedies, there is a prior question. Is this person an employee at all?
Get that wrong and everything after it is wasted. A well-argued unfair dismissal claim by someone who was never an employee fails on the first point.
This is also where the two Malaysian statutes can diverge. Scope is defined by each Act for its own purposes, and being covered by one does not mean being covered by the other.

sections.h: Why the contract's label is not decisive
sections.keypoint: If a label could decide status, the protections could be drafted away, so courts look at the substance of the relationship.

body.text: Many contracts say the person is an independent contractor. Some say it several times.
If that settled it, the protections would be optional. Any employer could draft its way out of the entire regime.
So the label is evidence of what the parties intended, and no more. The court looks at how the relationship actually worked.

body.prompt: A contract states clearly that the worker is not an employee, and both parties signed it knowingly. Does that settle status?
options: Yes — the parties are free to characterise their own relationship
No — otherwise the statutory protections could be removed by drafting
body.reveal: The reason is structural rather than paternalistic. A protection that a contract can switch off is not a protection, so the category has to be determined by what happened rather than by what the document says happened.

sections.h: What the courts actually look at
sections.keypoint: Control, integration into the business, and who bears the financial risk are the recurring indicators.

body.text: No single factor decides. The indicators recur, and they are worth knowing as a set.
Control: how far the other party directs not just what is done but how it is done.
Integration: whether the person is part of the business or provides services to it from outside.
Financial risk: who supplies the equipment, who can profit from doing the job efficiently, who bears the loss if it goes badly.

items: Can the person send a substitute, or must they perform personally?
Do they work for others at the same time?
Who decides when and where the work is done?
Are they paid for time, or for a result?

body.text: Apply them to facts rather than reciting them. A list of factors with no application to the problem earns nothing.

sections.h: Scope is set by each statute
sections.keypoint: Even a clear employee may be outside a particular Act, because each defines its own coverage.

body.text: There is a second trap after status. Being an employee is not the same as being covered by a given Act.
The statute setting minimum terms defines who it applies to, and that definition has its own conditions.
So an employee may have the protection of one regime and not the other. Check the scope provisions of the Act you are relying on, in the Act itself.

body.q: Your client is plainly an employee. Does it follow that the statutory minimum terms apply to them?
options: Not necessarily — that Act defines its own scope, and the definition has conditions
Yes — the Act protects employees
body.why: Status and coverage are separate questions. Establishing the first without checking the second produces advice that is right about the category and wrong about the entitlement.

quiz.q: Why is a contractual statement that someone is an independent contractor not decisive?
options: Because such clauses are unlawful
Because a protection that drafting could switch off would not be a protection
Because employees cannot read contracts
Because only the Industrial Court may decide status
quiz.why: The reason is structural. If the label decided the category, the whole statutory regime would be optional at the employer's election, so the substance of the relationship governs.

quiz.q: Which of these is a recognised indicator of employment status?
options: The job title
Whether the contract is in writing
Who bears the financial risk of the work
How long the relationship lasted
quiz.why: Financial risk sits alongside control and integration as a recurring indicator. Duration and formality may be evidence, but they are not the tests themselves.

reading.where: the provisions defining who the Act applies to — find them and read the conditions, because this lesson deliberately does not state a section number
the treatment of employment status and of the Act's scope

lessons.source: The employee and independent contractor distinction is standard doctrine applied in Malaysia; the scope of the statutory minimum terms is set by the Employment Act 1955. No section of that Act is stated here, because this corpus has not verified one.
lessons.verify: Find and read the scope provisions of the Employment Act 1955 in the current published version, and check the reprint's currency date. Confirm the conditions from the Act itself; this lesson names no section on purpose.

lessons.title: What a dismissal claim can actually produce
lessons.summary: A dismissal challenge does not undo the dismissal. Knowing what the process can and cannot deliver is what makes advice on it worth having.

sections.h: Start from the outcome
sections.keypoint: Clients choose a route by what it delivers and how long it takes, not by which doctrine is more elegant.

body.text: A dismissed client wants to know two things. What can I get, and how long will it take.
Doctrine answers neither directly, which is why advice that begins with doctrine so often misses.
Start from the outcome and work back. It also tests whether the route you are recommending is the right one.
A strong claim on a route that cannot deliver what the client needs is worse than a modest claim on one that can.

sections.h: The two limbs of a challenge
sections.keypoint: A dismissal can fail because there was no good reason, or because the process was wrong — and these are independent.

body.text: A challenge to a dismissal has a substantive limb and a procedural one.
The substantive question is whether there was a proper reason. The procedural question is whether the employer went about it properly.
They are independent. An employer with an excellent reason can lose on process, and an employer with an immaculate process can lose on reason.

body.prompt: An employer has clear evidence of serious misconduct but dismissed without giving the employee any chance to respond. What is the likely position?
options: The dismissal stands — the reason was plainly good
The reason may be good and the dismissal may still be successfully challenged on process
body.reveal: Treating a good reason as curing everything is the most common employer error and the most common student one. The two limbs are asked separately because they protect different things: one against being dismissed for nothing, the other against being dismissed without being heard.

body.text: In an answer, deal with them in separate paragraphs. Merging them hides which one you are relying on.

sections.h: What the process can order
sections.keypoint: Reinstatement is the primary remedy in principle, but compensation is the common outcome in practice.

body.text: The remedy most associated with this jurisdiction is being put back in the job.
In practice it is often not what happens. Relationships have broken down, positions have been filled, and time has passed.
So compensation is the usual outcome, and a client expecting their job back should be told early that it is not the likely result.
How compensation is calculated is set by the applicable rules and practice rather than by a formula you can derive. Check it rather than estimating.

body.q: Your client's first question is whether they will get their job back. What does honest advice look like?
options: Explain that it is the primary remedy in principle but compensation is the common outcome, and say why
Reassure them — reinstatement is the primary remedy
body.why: Both halves are true and the client needs both. Leading with the principle alone builds an expectation that the process is unlikely to meet, and that is the disappointment good advice exists to prevent.

sections.h: The deadline comes first
sections.keypoint: A time limit is the one thing later quality of advice cannot repair, so it belongs at the top of the letter.

body.text: There is a period within which a dismissal must be challenged, and missing it is usually fatal.
This is the single most consequential thing in the whole area, and it is routinely buried at the end of an advice letter.
Put it at the top. A client who reads only the first paragraph should still know the deadline exists.
And confirm the period in the instrument rather than from memory. A period stated wrongly is worse than no advice, because it will be relied on.
This lesson deliberately does not state the period. Find it in the Act, and note the date you checked it.

quiz.q: An employer has a clearly good reason but dismissed without any hearing. What is the position?
options: The dismissal is safe, because the reason was good
The employee must prove bad faith
The dismissal may still be successfully challenged, because the procedural limb is separate
Only the reason matters in Malaysian law
quiz.why: The substantive and procedural limbs are independent. Each protects something different, so satisfying one does not answer the other.

quiz.q: What should appear at the top of an advice letter on a dismissal?
options: The time limit for bringing the challenge
The strength of the merits
The employer's likely defence
The client's employment history
quiz.why: A missed deadline cannot be repaired by any later quality of advice, so it belongs where a frightened reader will see it even if they read nothing else.

the treatment of remedies, and of what happens in practice as against what the legislation provides for

lessons.source: The two limbs of a dismissal challenge and the remedial position are standard Malaysian industrial relations doctrine under the Industrial Relations Act 1967. No section and no time limit is stated here, because this corpus has not verified one.

lessons.title: Hours, rest days and overtime, and who they actually cover
lessons.summary: The Employment Act 1955 limits ordinary hours, guarantees a rest day, and requires extra pay for extra work. None of that helps a worker the Act does not cover.

sections.keypoint: Encik Halim's hours problem has two parts, and only one is about the number of hours.
sections.h: A long week in Klang

body.text: Encik Halim drives a delivery van out of a warehouse in Klang.
Some weeks he works every day, and often past dark.
His question sounds simple. Can my employer make me work like this?
It splits into two questions, and the split is where the law actually lives.

items: **Does the Act limit his hours at all?** That depends on rules about hours, rest and overtime.
**Does the Act apply to him?** That depends on rules about who counts, separate from the hours rules themselves.

sections.keypoint: Ordinary hours have a ceiling, a rest day is guaranteed, and extra work earns extra pay.
sections.h: What the Act actually protects

body.text: Where the Act applies, three protections sit alongside each other.
The Employment Act 1955 sets a ceiling on ordinary hours of work, requires a rest day in each week, and requires overtime to be paid at an enhanced rate above ordinary pay.
Each protection answers a different complaint.

items: A ceiling on hours answers *I am asked to work without end*.
A rest day answers *I never get a full day off*.
Enhanced overtime pay answers *I am paid the same for extra hours as ordinary ones*.

body.text: This lesson gives no figure for the hours ceiling, the overtime rate, or how a rest day is counted. Read the Act for the current figures.

sections.keypoint: The same Act that limits hours also decides, on its own terms, who gets that limit.
sections.h: Coverage is a separate gate

body.text: Being an employee is not the end of the enquiry.
The hours, rest day and overtime protections apply only within categories the Act sets for itself.
Coverage is often tied to the kind of work done, or how much is earned.
A worker can be plainly employed and still sit outside this particular part of the Act.
So the coverage question has to be checked provision by provision, not assumed from the job title.

sections.keypoint: A manager and a driver can work for the same firm and land on opposite sides of the same protection.
sections.h: Two workers, one warehouse

body.text: Puan Aisyah manages the same warehouse where Encik Halim drives.
Both are clearly employees. Neither question from earlier is in doubt for either of them.

body.prompt: Does it follow that the hours, rest day and overtime rules apply to Puan Aisyah the same way they apply to Encik Halim?
options: Yes — both are employees, so both get the same protection
Not necessarily — the Act may draw its own line between them by role or pay
No — only drivers are ever covered by hours protections
body.reveal: The Act's hours provisions carve out their own coverage, often by the nature of the work or the pay involved. A manager and a driver at the same firm can land on different sides of that line, even though both are employees.

lessons.source: The existence of hours, rest day and overtime protections, and the fact that coverage is set separately by the Employment Act 1955, is standard doctrine. No figure, ceiling or rate is stated here, because this corpus has not verified one.
lessons.verify: This lesson states no section number, no hours figure, and no rate for X on purpose; confirm it in the current Employment Act 1955 as published by the Attorney General's Chambers and record the date you checked.

lessons.title: Pregnancy at work, and the dismissal it is not supposed to trigger
lessons.summary: The Employment Act 1955 gives eligible employees paid maternity leave, and a dismissal tangled up with pregnancy runs straight into the unjust dismissal system. Timing is evidence, not proof by itself.

sections.keypoint: A dismissal that lands right after a pregnancy announcement raises a question the calendar alone cannot answer.
sections.h: Two events, close together

body.text: Kak Zurina works at a bakery in Ipoh.
She tells her employer she is pregnant. Soon after, she is told her post is being closed.
She wants to know two things. Is she owed leave and pay around the birth? And was the timing of her dismissal a coincidence?
Both questions matter, and they are answered by different parts of the law.

sections.keypoint: Paid maternity leave is a statutory entitlement for an eligible employee, with conditions the Act sets for itself.
sections.h: The leave entitlement

body.text: The Employment Act 1955 gives an eligible female employee paid maternity leave around the birth of a child, subject to conditions the Act sets for eligibility.
Eligibility is not automatic for every pregnant employee.
The Act sets its own conditions, and those conditions have to be checked rather than assumed.
No length of leave, no qualifying period, and no rate of pay is stated here. Confirm every figure against the current Act.

sections.keypoint: A dismissal tied to pregnancy is a strong candidate for a claim of dismissal without just cause or excuse.
sections.h: Where dismissal law joins in

body.text: Dismissing an employee because she is pregnant does not sit inside the maternity leave rules at all.
It sits inside the separate system for challenging a dismissal without just cause or excuse.
The Industrial Relations Act 1967 lets a workman challenge a dismissal without just cause or excuse, and a reason connected to pregnancy is unlikely to be treated as a genuine one.
So a pregnant employee who is dismissed may have two live matters, not one: leave and pay already owed, and a separate challenge to the dismissal itself.
An employer who dismisses Zurina for 'restructuring' the same week she announces her pregnancy has handed her a strong fact pattern. It is not a defence that ends the enquiry.

sections.keypoint: Timing that looks suspicious still has to be tested against the employer's actual reason, not assumed to prove it.
sections.h: Suspicion is a starting point, not a verdict

body.text: Close timing between an announcement and a dismissal invites suspicion. It does not, by itself, decide the case.
An employer can have a genuine, unrelated reason that happens to land at an awkward moment.

body.q: Zurina is dismissed soon after telling her employer she is pregnant. What is the right next step in advising her?
options: Examine whether the stated reason for dismissal was genuine, using the timing as one piece of evidence among others
Treat the timing as conclusive proof the dismissal was because of the pregnancy
Advise her that only the maternity leave rules are relevant, since she has already been dismissed
body.why: Timing is evidence that invites scrutiny of the employer's stated reason. It is not a substitute for testing whether that reason was real, which is exactly what the unjust dismissal enquiry does.

lessons.source: Maternity leave as a distinct statutory entitlement under the Employment Act 1955, and the availability of an unjust dismissal challenge under the Industrial Relations Act 1967 where a dismissal is connected to pregnancy, are standard doctrine. No period, qualifying condition or rate is stated here, because this corpus has not verified one.
lessons.verify: This lesson states no section number, no leave period, and no eligibility condition for X on purpose; confirm it in the current Employment Act 1955 and Industrial Relations Act 1967 as published by the Attorney General's Chambers and record the date you checked.

lessons.title: Termination benefits, and why they are not the same claim as unjust dismissal
lessons.summary: A payment for losing a job through no fault of the employee is a different claim from compensation for a dismissal without just cause or excuse. An employer meeting one does not automatically meet the other.

sections.keypoint: One payment is about the job disappearing. A separate claim is about whether the dismissal itself was lawful.
sections.h: A closed factory in Melaka

body.text: En. Farid's factory in Melaka shuts its doors. Nobody says he did anything wrong.
He is told he will receive a payment for losing his job this way.
He also wonders whether he can still challenge the dismissal itself.
Both questions can be true at once, and confusing them costs a client money.

sections.keypoint: Regulations under the Employment Act 1955 give benefits for termination and lay-off, tied to service rather than fault.
sections.h: A payment for no fault at all

body.text: Regulations made under the Employment Act 1955 provide for termination and lay-off benefits, payable to an eligible employee whose employment ends through redundancy, closure or lay-off rather than through their own fault.
The idea behind this payment is not punishment of the employer.
It recognises that losing a job through no fault of your own still costs the person who lost it.
No formula, no qualifying length of service, and no scale of payment is given here. Read the regulations themselves for the current figures.

sections.keypoint: One claim is for a fixed payment tied to service. The other is for whether the dismissal itself had just cause.
sections.h: A different claim, a different question

body.text: Compensation for a dismissal without just cause or excuse is not the same pot of money.
That claim asks whether the reason for dismissal was genuine and whether the process was fair, under the Industrial Relations Act 1967.

body.caption: Two claims that sound alike and are not
rows: Termination or lay-off benefit
Has service ended through redundancy, closure or lay-off?
The job ending, regardless of who is at fault.
Unjust dismissal compensation
Was there just cause or excuse, reached by a fair process?
A dismissal the employee says was wrong or unfairly handled.
body.alt: Two claims side by side. A termination or lay-off benefit asks only whether service ended through redundancy, closure or lay-off, and is triggered by the job ending regardless of fault. Unjust dismissal compensation asks whether there was just cause or excuse reached by a fair process. It is triggered by a dismissal the employee says was wrong or unfairly handled.

sections.keypoint: Paying one claim does not close the other, though what is actually owed on each may end up connected in practice.
sections.h: Does paying one claim close the other?

body.text: An employer who has already paid a termination benefit sometimes argues that settles everything.

body.prompt: Farid receives his termination benefit and later wants to argue the whole redundancy exercise was not genuine. Does the payment stop him?
options: No — the two claims are legally distinct, whatever weight the payment is later given
Yes — accepting the payment always waives any further claim
Only if he signed a release naming his employer
body.reveal: The benefit and the unjust dismissal claim answer different questions, so paying one does not, by itself, answer the other. What is actually owed once both claims are established is a separate matter. The current position on any set-off belongs in the Act and current practice, not in assumption.

lessons.source: The existence of termination and lay-off benefits under regulations made under the Employment Act 1955, and their separateness from unjust dismissal compensation under the Industrial Relations Act 1967, are standard doctrine. No figure, formula or qualifying period is stated here, because this corpus has not verified one.
lessons.verify: This lesson states no section number, no regulation number, and no payment figure for X on purpose; confirm it in the current Employment Act 1955, its regulations, and the Industrial Relations Act 1967 as published by the Attorney General's Chambers, and record the date you checked.

lessons.title: Retrenchment, and why last in, first out is a guideline, not a rule
lessons.summary: Retrenchment is dismissal because a role has genuinely disappeared, and it can still be challenged if the reason is not real or the selection is unfair. Last in, first out is a common yardstick for fairness, not a formula the law commands.

sections.keypoint: Losing a job to a genuine redundancy still leaves two things worth checking before accepting it.
sections.h: Half a shift, gone

body.text: Cik Yusof has worked at a plastics plant in Johor Bahru for several years.
The plant retrenches half of one shift. Yusof is among them.
Retrenchment is dismissal because a role has genuinely disappeared, not because of anything Yusof did.
That does not put it beyond challenge. Two questions still need asking.

items: **Was the redundancy genuine?** Has the role actually gone, or is 'retrenchment' covering something else?
**Was the selection fair?** Given that some roles went and some stayed, why was Yusof one of the ones chosen?

sections.keypoint: The Industrial Relations Act 1967 lets the Industrial Court test both whether a redundancy was genuine and whether the selection was fair.
sections.h: Where retrenchment sits in dismissal law

body.text: The Industrial Relations Act 1967 allows a retrenchment dismissal to be challenged as one without just cause or excuse, examining both whether the redundancy was genuine and whether the employee selected was chosen fairly.
The Act does not set out a fixed formula for choosing who goes.
What it asks for is a genuine reason and a fair method, which is the same two-limb pattern this whole module keeps returning to.

sections.keypoint: Seniority-based selection is a familiar and often-accepted yardstick, but the law does not command it in every case.
sections.h: Last in, first out, and its limits

body.text: A common convention is to let go of the most recently hired employees first.
This is usually called last in, first out, and it is a familiar starting point in a retrenchment exercise.
It is a convention, not a command. An employer can depart from it for a genuine, objective reason, such as a skill the business still needs.

Yusof has less seniority than several colleagues, but he is the only one certified to run a machine the plant depends on. Keeping him and letting more senior colleagues go can still be a fair selection.
A departure from seniority still has to be genuine and applied consistently. A reason invented after the selection was already made will not save it.

sections.keypoint: Neither strict seniority nor a departure from it is automatically fair — both still have to be tested against the facts.
sections.h: Testing a selection either way

body.text: Two wrong instincts sit on either side of this topic.
One treats last in, first out as a rule that must always be followed. The other treats any departure from it as automatically suspicious.

body.q: An employer departs from strict seniority and keeps a junior employee with a scarce skill instead of a more senior one. Is the selection automatically unfair?
options: Yes — departing from last in, first out is always unfair
It is automatically fair, because employers may always choose based on skill
No — the selection is fair only if the stated skill reason is genuine and was applied consistently
body.why: Neither extreme is right. Last in, first out is a guideline the Industrial Court often treats as fair evidence. Departing from it is neither forbidden nor automatically safe — the genuine reason still has to be shown and applied consistently.

lessons.source: Retrenchment as a species of dismissal challengeable under the Industrial Relations Act 1967, and last in, first out as an accepted but non-mandatory convention for selection, are standard Malaysian industrial relations doctrine. No section number is stated here, because this corpus has not verified one.
lessons.verify: This lesson states no section number for X on purpose; confirm it in the current Industrial Relations Act 1967 as published by the Attorney General's Chambers and record the date you checked.

lessons.title: What a seller promises about title and quality
lessons.summary: When you buy goods in Malaysia, the law reads certain promises into the sale even if nobody says them aloud. A seller who cannot show good title, or who hands over defective goods, breaks the contract whether or not a clause said so.

sections.keypoint: Selling something you never owned breaks a promise, even if nobody wrote the promise down.
sections.h: A laptop a shop never owned

body.text: En Razak runs a small electronics shop in Ipoh, buying and reselling secondhand laptops.
He sells a laptop to Mei Ling for RM1,200. Two months later, the police seize it as stolen property.
Razak never owned that laptop. He could not pass good title to Mei Ling, whatever the receipt said.
Malaysian law does not wait for a written promise here. It reads one into the sale automatically.

sections.keypoint: One old statute quietly writes four promises into a sale, whether the parties mention them or not.
sections.h: Four promises the Act reads into every sale

body.text: The Sale of Goods Act 1957 is old and short, but it still does heavy work today.

A contract for the sale of goods carries terms the parties never had to write down. The seller must actually have the right to sell the goods. Goods sold by description must match that description. Goods sold in the course of a business must be of acceptable quality, and must suit any particular purpose the buyer made known to the seller.

body.caption: Four implied promises behind an ordinary sale
rows: Title
That the seller can actually sell the goods
Razak did not own the stolen laptop
Description
That goods match how they were described
A phone sold as 'new' turns out used
Quality
That goods are of acceptable quality
A rice cooker that never switches on
Fitness for purpose
That goods suit a purpose the buyer named
A cable sold 'for this printer' that does not fit it
body.alt: Four implied promises in a sale. Title: the seller can actually sell the goods, as Razak could not for a stolen laptop. Description: goods match how they were described, so a phone sold as new must not be used. Quality: goods are of acceptable quality, so a rice cooker that never switches on fails this. Fitness for purpose: goods suit a purpose the buyer named, so a cable sold for a named printer must fit it.

body.text: None of this needs a clause. The Act puts these promises into the sale by itself.

sections.keypoint: A seller can disclaim quality complaints in the price, but cannot sell what was never theirs to sell.
sections.h: Why 'sold as is' does not fix a title problem

body.text: Shops sometimes mark secondhand goods 'sold as is', hoping to escape complaints later.
That phrase can fairly cover wear, scratches, or a missing accessory the buyer could see for themselves.
It does not cover the right to sell in the first place. Razak could not have fixed that with a sign.

body.prompt: Razak's shop has a sign saying 'all sales final, sold as is'. Does that sign protect him from Mei Ling's claim over the stolen laptop?
options: Yes — the sign covers every complaint about the goods
No — a disclaimer about condition does not cure a missing right to sell
Only if Mei Ling read the sign before buying
body.reveal: Title and quality are different promises. A disclaimer aimed at condition does not reach a defect in Razak's right to sell the laptop at all.

sections.keypoint: A broken promise about title or quality is an ordinary breach, with an ordinary buyer's remedy.
sections.h: What Mei Ling can do about it

body.text: Mei Ling's laptop is gone, seized as stolen property. She still has a claim.
A broken promise under the Sale of Goods Act is a breach of contract like any other.
She can claim back what she paid, plus compensation for her loss.
That question is answered by the general law of contract, covered elsewhere in this module.

body.q: Mei Ling wants her RM1,200 back and something for the trouble caused. Which law question is she really asking?
options: A criminal question only the police can answer
An ordinary breach of contract question, once the implied term is shown to be broken
A question with no legal answer, since the goods are already gone
body.why: Once the implied term about title is shown to be broken, this becomes an ordinary claim for breach of contract, with the questions about what compensation follows.

quiz.q: Razak's shop sells a laptop it never owned. Which implied promise is broken?
options: The promise that goods match their description
The promise that the seller has the right to sell the goods
The promise that goods are of acceptable quality
quiz.why: Title is the promise that the seller actually has the right to sell. Razak never owned the laptop, so he broke this promise regardless of its condition.

quiz.q: A shop's sign says 'sold as is'. Which of these can that phrase fairly cover?
options: A missing right to sell the goods at all
Any defect whatsoever, no matter how hidden
Wear and visible defects the buyer could see for themself
quiz.why: A disclaimer about condition can fairly cover wear and visible defects. It cannot cure a missing right to sell in the first place.

lessons.source: Sale of Goods Act 1957 for the implied terms; no case is cited, and no section number is stated for the Act on purpose.
lessons.verify: This lesson deliberately states no section number for the seller's implied undertakings on title, description, quality and fitness for purpose; confirm each in the current Sale of Goods Act 1957 as published by the Attorney General's Chambers and record the date you checked.

lessons.title: Hire purchase, and what happens when you fall behind
lessons.summary: A hire-purchase agreement lets a small business get a vehicle or machine without paying the full price upfront. Miss enough payments, and the owner's right to take the goods back is not as simple as just walking in and taking them.

sections.keypoint: The finance company owns the van until every instalment is paid, even though the caterer drives it daily.
sections.h: A catering van bought on hire purchase

body.text: Puan Zaleha runs a small catering business in Shah Alam. She needs a van to deliver orders.
She cannot pay RM60,000 outright, so she buys the van on hire purchase from a finance company instead.
Zaleha uses the van every day. Legally, the finance company still owns it until she pays the last instalment.
That gap between using something and owning it is exactly what a hire-purchase agreement creates.

sections.keypoint: The Hire Purchase Act sets required content and formalities that an ordinary loan agreement does not need.
sections.h: What the Act actually protects

body.text: Hire purchase is common enough that Parliament gave it its own statute.

A hire-purchase agreement must be in writing, and the hirer must be given a copy of it. The Act sets out required content for the agreement, and gives a hirer specific protections that an ordinary loan or ordinary sale does not carry.
Those protections exist because a hirer can lose the goods, and any instalments already paid, if things go wrong.

items: The agreement must set out the cash price, the hire-purchase price, and the instalments.
A hirer is normally given some minimum period to put the account right.
The owner's power to repossess is not unlimited once a hirer has paid a meaningful share of the price.

sections.keypoint: Once a hirer has paid a real share of the price, repossession without a court's help is restricted.
sections.h: Why the owner cannot just take the van back

body.text: Zaleha misses three months of payments. The finance company wants the van back immediately.

This lesson does not state the exact share of the price, or the exact procedure, that limits repossession. Confirm the current threshold and process in the Hire Purchase Act 1967 itself, since this is exactly the kind of detail that must be checked rather than assumed.
The general shape of the protection is well known: paying a substantial part of the price changes what the owner may do next.

body.prompt: Zaleha has paid more than half the total price when she falls behind. Can the finance company simply seize the van itself, with no court involved?
options: Yes — missing a payment always allows immediate seizure
Not necessarily — paying a substantial share can require a court's involvement first
Only if the van is parked in a public place
body.reveal: Malaysian hire-purchase law limits self-help repossession once a hirer has paid a meaningful share of the price. Read the current threshold and procedure in the Act before advising anyone on it.

sections.keypoint: Repossession does not simply cancel out everything a hirer already paid toward the goods.
sections.h: The instalments already paid are not automatically lost

body.text: Suppose the van is repossessed anyway, properly this time, following the correct process.
Zaleha has already paid RM25,000 toward a van now back with the finance company.
Whether she can recover any of that, and how any shortfall on resale is settled, is set by the Act's own rules, not by guesswork.

body.q: Zaleha wants to know if her RM25,000 in instalments simply disappears once the van is repossessed. What is the honest answer?
options: Yes, all instalments are automatically forfeited
It is settled by the Act's own accounting rules, which must be checked rather than assumed
No, she automatically gets every instalment back in full
body.why: The Hire Purchase Act sets its own rules for what happens to instalments already paid. Neither automatic forfeiture nor automatic full refund is a safe assumption without reading them.

quiz.q: Zaleha's hire-purchase agreement is not in writing at all. What does the Act say about that?
options: It has no requirements about form
The agreement must be in writing, with a copy given to the hirer
Only oral agreements are enforceable in hire purchase
quiz.why: The Hire Purchase Act requires a written agreement, with a copy given to the hirer. This lesson does not state which section sets that out.

quiz.q: After three months of missed payments, can a finance company always seize hire-purchase goods without any court step?
options: No — paying a substantial share of the price can require a court's involvement
Yes, missing any payment removes every protection immediately
Only for vehicles, never for machinery
quiz.why: Once a hirer has paid a meaningful share of the price, self-help repossession is restricted. Confirm the exact threshold in the current Act.

lessons.source: Hire Purchase Act 1967 for the form of the agreement and for repossession; no case is cited, and no section number is stated for the Act on purpose.
lessons.verify: This lesson states no section number for the required form of a hire-purchase agreement, for repossession, or for what happens to instalments already paid, on purpose; confirm each in the current Hire Purchase Act 1967 as published by the Attorney General's Chambers and record the date you checked.

lessons.title: How a cheque actually works as a promise to pay
lessons.summary: A cheque looks like a piece of paper, but the law treats it as an order to a bank to pay money. Understanding what kind of order it is explains why a bounced cheque, and a stolen one, behave so differently.

sections.keypoint: A cheque is not money changing hands. It is an order that a bank must be asked to honour.
sections.h: A caterer paid with a cheque that bounces

body.text: Puan Aminah runs a small catering business in Melaka. A client pays her RM4,000 with a cheque.
Aminah deposits it. Three days later, the bank returns it, marked 'refer to drawer' — the client's account has insufficient funds.
Aminah has not been paid. She has been handed an order to pay that the bank refused to carry out.
That is the entire nature of a cheque. It is a promise wrapped inside an instruction to someone else.

sections.keypoint: A cheque is simply a bill of exchange payable on demand and drawn on a bank.
sections.h: What a bill of exchange actually is

body.text: The law behind this sits in an old statute most people never read: the Bills of Exchange Act 1949.

A bill of exchange is a written, unconditional order by one person to another, signed by the person giving it, requiring the person to whom it is addressed to pay a sum of money to a named person, or to bearer, on demand or at a fixed or determinable future time. A cheque is a bill of exchange drawn on a bank and payable on demand.
Three parties usually appear: the drawer who writes it, the drawee bank asked to pay, and the payee who is meant to receive the money.

body.caption: The three parties to a cheque
rows: Drawer
The person who writes and signs the cheque
Aminah's client
Drawee
The bank asked to pay out
The client's bank
Payee
The person meant to receive the money
Aminah
body.alt: Three parties to a cheque. The drawer writes and signs it — here, Aminah's client. The drawee is the bank asked to pay out — the client's bank. The payee is meant to receive the money — Aminah herself.

sections.keypoint: Signing the back of a cheque can pass the right to be paid on to someone else entirely.
sections.h: Why endorsing a cheque matters

body.text: Aminah could have signed the back of that cheque over to her supplier, instead of banking it herself.
That signature is called an endorsement. It can pass the right to receive payment to a new holder.
This lesson does not name a section for endorsement, negotiation, or holder in due course. Confirm each in the current Bills of Exchange Act 1949 before relying on it.

body.prompt: Aminah endorses the cheque to her supplier, who takes it without knowing it will bounce. Can the supplier still demand payment from Aminah if it does?
options: No — once endorsed, Aminah has no further responsibility for it
Only if the supplier is a bank
Usually yes — an endorser can still be liable if the cheque is dishonoured
body.reveal: Endorsing a cheque passes it on, but it does not automatically wash the endorser's hands of it. Confirm the current rules on an endorser's liability before advising on any real cheque.

sections.keypoint: Someone who takes a cheque properly and in good faith can end up better protected than the original owner.
sections.h: A stolen cheque, and who ends up bearing the loss

body.text: Suppose a cheque payable to Aminah is stolen, and the thief manages to cash it.
Who bears that loss can depend on whether the person who took the cheque did so properly and in good faith, for value.
This is the idea behind a 'holder in due course' — a status the Act protects specially.

body.q: A thief negotiates a stolen cheque to a shopkeeper who takes it in good faith and gives value for it. What question decides who bears the loss?
options: Whether the shopkeeper is a registered business
Whether the shopkeeper qualifies as a holder in due course
Whether the police ever catch the thief
body.why: The protection given to a genuine holder in due course is exactly the doctrine built to answer this question. This lesson does not name the section; check it in the current Act.

quiz.q: Which of these is Aminah's cheque, in the language of the Bills of Exchange Act?
options: A bill of exchange payable on demand, drawn on a bank
A simple IOU with no special legal status
A form of cash that transfers ownership instantly
quiz.why: A cheque is defined as a bill of exchange drawn on a bank and payable on demand. That single sentence is the whole of what a cheque legally is.

quiz.q: A cheque bounces marked 'refer to drawer'. What has actually happened, in legal terms?
options: The cheque has become void and can never be presented again
The payee has automatically lost all rights against the drawer
The bank has dishonoured an order it was asked to pay
quiz.why: Dishonour means the bank refused to carry out the order. The payee's rights against the drawer are not automatically wiped out by that refusal.

lessons.source: Bills of Exchange Act 1949 for the nature of a cheque, endorsement and holder in due course; no case is cited, and no section number is stated for the Act on purpose.

lessons.title: Whether a website's terms bind a customer who never read them
lessons.summary: An online shop's terms and conditions sit behind a link nobody clicks. Malaysian contract law still has to decide when clicking 'buy' creates a binding agreement, and on whose terms.

sections.keypoint: A website order still has to go through the ordinary steps of offer and acceptance.
sections.h: An online order that seemed simple

body.text: Encik Firdaus runs a small online store from Johor Bahru, selling handmade furniture.
A customer, Puan Noraini, adds a table to her cart and clicks 'Place Order'. She pays instantly by card.
The table arrives three weeks later than the website promised. Noraini wants to cancel and get a refund.
Firdaus points to his terms and conditions page, which she never opened. Is she bound by it anyway?

sections.keypoint: The Contracts Act's rules on offer and acceptance were written for letters, and now apply to clicks.
sections.h: The old rules still apply to the click

body.text: Malaysian contract law does not have a separate rulebook for websites. It applies the same Act it always has.

Section 2(a) treats a proposal as one person showing another that they are willing to do something, in order to get that other person's agreement to it. That is what an offer is, whether it is spoken, written, or clicked.
Whether Firdaus's website is making an offer, or only inviting Noraini to make one, is the first question to answer.

Section 4 sets out when a proposal, an acceptance, and a revocation are each treated as communicated. A proposal is communicated once it reaches the knowledge of the person it is made to; an acceptance is communicated at a moment the section itself fixes.
These rules were built for letters and telegrams. They still have to answer questions a screen and a server now raise.

sections.keypoint: A proposal can usually be withdrawn before acceptance is complete, which is why timing decides so much online.
sections.h: When can Firdaus still pull the listing?

body.text: Suppose Firdaus's website lists the table at RM200 by mistake — a typing error, meant to read RM2,000.
Noraini orders it at RM200 before anyone notices. Can Firdaus simply cancel once he spots the error?

Section 5 allows a proposal to be revoked at any time before the communication of its acceptance is complete as against the proposer, but not afterwards. The same timing rule applies to revoking an acceptance.
So the real question is not fairness. It is timing — was Firdaus's proposal revoked before Noraini's acceptance became complete?

body.prompt: Firdaus's site auto-confirms every order the instant 'Place Order' is clicked, before any human checks it. Does that change when the contract is formed?
options: Yes — the moment communication of acceptance is complete can arrive earlier than a human review step
No — automation is irrelevant, only a court can fix the moment
It changes nothing, because typing errors always void a sale
body.reveal: An instant, automatic confirmation can complete the communication of acceptance sooner than a business expects. That is a timing point, not a fairness point, and it is where many online-pricing disputes actually turn.

sections.keypoint: A term buried behind an unopened link may not have been properly brought to the customer's notice at all.
sections.h: Terms nobody clicked on

body.text: Noraini never opened Firdaus's terms and conditions page before paying.
The Electronic Commerce Act 2006 recognises that a contract can be made and signed electronically, and does not strike that down for being electronic.
It does not, by itself, decide whether one particular clause was properly brought to a customer's attention.

This lesson states no section number for the Electronic Commerce Act 2006 on purpose. Confirm the current provisions in the Act itself, as published by the Attorney General's Chambers, and record the date you checked.
The older question still does the real work: was the term given reasonably enough notice before the customer agreed?

body.q: Firdaus wants a refund clause buried at the bottom of a page nobody has to open before paying to bind every customer. What is the honest answer?
options: Yes automatically, because it is written down somewhere on the site
It might not, unless the term was given reasonably enough notice before the customer agreed
No — website terms can never bind anyone in Malaysia
body.why: Putting a term online is not the same as giving reasonable notice of it. Whether Noraini is bound turns on notice, not on where the clause happened to be published.

quiz.q: Under section 2(a) of the Contracts Act, what does it take to make a proposal?
options: Sending a written contract signed by both parties
Signifying willingness to do or not do something, to get the other party's assent to it
Making a payment in advance
quiz.why: Section 2(a) defines a proposal exactly this way. It says nothing about the medium, so a website listing can qualify just as a letter can.

quiz.q: Which question actually decides whether Firdaus can withdraw the RM200 listing after Noraini orders it?
options: Whether Firdaus's revocation came before the communication of Noraini's acceptance was complete
Whether Firdaus later feels the price was unfair
Whether the website looks professionally designed
quiz.why: Section 5 ties revocation to a specific moment: before acceptance is complete. Everything else, including how the mistake happened, is beside that point.
